args.guideSection:
## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Texas was admitted to the Union on 29 December 1845 as the 28th state, created from the Republic of Texas (per the FamilySearch Wiki home page, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Texas,_United_States_Genealogy).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Austin is the capital (same Wiki page). The state has 254 counties.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States.
- **Population during period:** The survey returned only United States national population figures (for example 1980: 229,858,655 per the survey's population part); no Texas-specific figures were returned.
- **Economy:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Ethnic composition:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Religious denominations:** Not confirmed by this survey for 1962-2010.
- **Key historical events:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Coverage of this survey:** The digitized-volume part timed out on both attempts, so no volume counts are available. The Catalog reports 10,070 hits for the Texas place label, mostly county and local histories, not death registers.

## Boundary changes
- The survey returned no boundary changes for the state of Texas during 1962-2010. Statewide boundaries were not reported as changed in any tool result.
- Local registration by cities and towns from 1873 (per the Texas Research Tips page) means death records may exist at a municipal level as well as statewide; the survey did not identify which municipalities kept them.

## Research tips
- **Search order:** Start with the FamilySearch index collections that are free and cover the 1962-2010 window: Texas, Deaths, 1977-1986 (collection 1930157, index and images), then Texas Death Index, 1964-1998 (1375599) and Texas Death Index, 1903-2000 (1949337), both index only. Use these to find the death year and county. Then order the state certificate from the Texas Department of Health Bureau of Vital Statistics, Austin, which the Texas Vital Records page describes as the source when a record is not found online (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Texas_Vital_Records).
- **Statewide registration date:** The Texas Vital Records page says statewide registration of births and deaths began in 1903 with the formation of the Texas Department of Public Health; the Texas Research Tips page says statewide registration began in 1908 and was generally complied with by the 1930s (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Texas_Research_Tips_and_Strategies). The two pages disagree; the 1903 date is the one the Vital Records page gives.
- **Subscription sources:** Texas Death Certificates, 1903-1982 (Ancestry) and Texas Death Certificates, 1890-1976 (Fold3) are index and images but paid (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Texas_Online_Genealogy_Records).
- **Substitute records:** The Research Tips page names obituaries as substitutes for parents and family details; its Texas Newspapers and Texas Obituaries pages were not read by this survey (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Texas_Research_Tips_and_Strategies).
- **Gaps:** The FamilySearch Wiki question-specific search timed out, and the survey's digitized-volume part timed out. Treat the absence of any further Texas death-specific guidance as unconfirmed.

Either may state the death date and place directly. Their facts are to be extracted, and the searches below verify or replace them. Neither file has extracted text yet, so this item is not yet read.

Texas Death Index, 1964-1998 (FamilySearch 1375599) is name-searchable and gives a death year and county for a Texas death. It gives no certificate image, so a hit must be confirmed on the certificate (item 9). The tree records a move to Los Angeles, California on 2 July 1962, so a Texas death is not assumed.
Texas Death Index, 1903-2000 (FamilySearch 1949337) is name-searchable and spans the 1964-1998 index plus 1999-2000. Fallback for item 2 if that index returns no entry for Kenneth Werner Quass.

Texas, Deaths, 1977-1986 (FamilySearch 1930157) is name-searchable with certificate images, so it can show the death place and date directly rather than only an index entry. Covers the early part of the 1962-2010 window.

United States, Social Security Death Index (FamilySearch 1202535), name-searchable, covers the full 1962-2010 window and is not limited to Texas. It can show a death in any state, so it locates the death place without assuming Texas; the 1962 Los Angeles move makes California a live possibility. Its listing gives a state and a date, which then direct the Texas or California searches.

United States, GenealogyBank Obituaries, Births, and Marriages, 1980-2015 (FamilySearch 2333694) is name-searchable. An obituary would name the death place and date, and any survivors listed would be FAN leads. Covers the late part of the window.

BillionGraves Index (FamilySearch 2026973) is name-searchable and holds burial-marker transcriptions, which can give a death year and place. Run it to find a burial that a death index does not show, even if a Find a Grave page was uploaded (item 1).

Texas Death Certificates, 1903-1982 (Ancestry, subscription, index and images) is the paid source the Texas guide names for certificate images. It is an external-site item, not a FamilySearch search, and is run only if the FamilySearch items leave the death place open.

JEANNE

MAY 26, 1914 - MAY 24, 2005

### **[Biographical Text]**

The information on the death certificate as place of death is false. Kenneth Werner died en-route from Miami, Florida to his home in San Diego, California, on a commercial airline. He was found dead in the rear toilet of the plane and his remains were placed in the last seat of the plane covered with a blanket until the plane landed at the downtown Dallas airport. I confirmed this with the airline he was the passenger on to thank them for their respectful treatment of my father's remains. He was dead upon arrival, but the coroner did not do an autopsy as required. He called Ken's son, the author of this bit of information, after talking with Ken's wife and asked some health questions as well as Kenneth W Quass' occupation. Kenneth was a national sales representative for several foreign auto parts manufacturers and was returning home from an extended visit with foreign auto parts suppliers and vehicle repair shops along the east coast of the USA. As a national sales representative, he had many friends and acquaintances in the USA. The coroner glibly put down as Ken's occupation as in 'auto sales' implying not of much importance an never performed an autopsy as federal law requires when one passes on a commercial airline. The coroner simply made an assumption as to the cause of death and noted the place of death as though it happened on the ground in Dallas. He then forged my signature on the death certificate as the informant. I resided in Minnesota at that time. In effect, Ken's cause of death is unknown. At his funeral, a close friend of the family aske me if an autopsy had been performed. I said no,, and he replied you may wish one had been done, for he was well aware of my father's health. A year or so later a Minnesota based foreign auto parts supplier approached me to ask if I knew what my father died of. I said no, He replied if I had ever thought of foul play. He proceeded to offer 'facts' that would support foul play at the Miami airport. I won't go into that with this bit of information, but it proved quite plausible.

entry.description: Place of death of Kenneth Werner Quass on 17 Sep 1982: Grapevine, Tarrant County, Texas (Texas death certificate 76852 and its Texas Death Index row) versus a Find a Grave biography that calls the certificate place false and says he died aboard a commercial flight from Miami to San Diego, was found dead in the aircraft toilet, and reached a Dallas-area airport with no autopsy.
entry.independence_analysis: Three assertions bear on the place, but they form two evidence units. The Texas Death Index row (a_003) is an index entry drawn from the same death certificate 76852 as the Ancestry transcription (a_013), so the row is not a second confirmation. The Find a Grave memorial's place field (a_027, Grapevine) matches the certificate and was likely copied from it, so it is not independent on place. Its only contrary content is the biographical text, written in the first person by the decedent's son, who says he was in Minnesota, was not present, and relied on an airline's confirmation and a coroner's telephone call. That informant chain does not overlap the certificate's named informant, but the son also alleges that the certificate's informant signature was forged, so the certificate's informant line is itself contested by the memorial. Two independent units therefore bear on place: the certificate unit and the memorial's biography.
entry.weighing_analysis: Relevance: the certificate is the record created to state where and how a death occurred, so it bears directly on place of death. Category and format: a state death certificate made under official duty at the time is the stronger category, but the copy in hand is an Ancestry transcription of index-level fields, and the uploaded certificate file has no extracted text, so its fidelity to the original is unverified. Informant proximity: the certifying official acted at the death; the memorial author learned the details secondhand, about 28 years later, from an airline and the coroner. Motive: the author alleges a forged signature, a negligent coroner, and foul play, a clear reason to contest the official record. Consistency: the memorial keeps Grapevine in its own header and contradicts it only in narrative. Plausibility: an in-flight death followed by landing at DFW, which adjoins Grapevine, is possible in 1982, so plausibility does not discredit the memorial. What decides it is corroboration and motive: no document in the project supports the flight, the no-autopsy claim, or the forgery. Limit: no document in hand excludes death aboard the aircraft. Only the airline's passenger or death report or the medical examiner's file for that flight could test it.
entry.resolution_rationale: 1. Problem: where Kenneth Werner Quass died on 17 Sep 1982 is disputed, and the answer sets the place the conclusion will state. 2. Evidence: Texas death certificate 76852, read through an Ancestry transcription, and its matching Texas Death Index row both record Grapevine, Tarrant County, Texas. The Find a Grave memorial's header agrees, but its biographical text, written in 2010 by the decedent's son, says that place is false, that he died aboard a commercial flight from Miami to San Diego, was found dead in the aircraft toilet, and that the remains reached a Dallas-area airport with no autopsy. The son was in Minnesota and reports the airline's and coroner's statements secondhand, and he alleges a forged informant signature. 3. Weighing: the certificate is the official record made at the time under the certifying official's duty. The memorial's contrary account is decades-removed hearsay from a person with a stated motive to contest the official record. Its flight claim is an uncorroborated single item, and the memorial keeps Grapevine in its own header. The certificate's recorded place is therefore preferred. 4. Why the other exists: the official plausibly recorded the place where the body was taken into custody, which for a death aboard a plane landing near Grapevine is a natural entry for the place of death. The son, not present, reports what he was told, and an in-flight death may have reached him only through the airline's account.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Question
When and where did Kenneth Werner Quass (born 4 December 1917, Iowa) die?

## Conclusion
The evidence indicates, at a probable level, that Kenneth Werner Quass died on 17 September 1982 at Grapevine, Tarrant County, Texas, as recorded on Texas death certificate 76852. The date is firmer than the place. The place is disputed by an untested family account described below; that dispute is open and is not settled by this conclusion.

*Content note: the dispute concerns the circumstances of a death, including an allegation of an unexamined death aboard an aircraft, a forged signature and possible foul play. These are one family member's claims and are uncorroborated.*

## Evidence for the date
Three sources give 17 September 1982. (1) Texas death certificate 76852, read as the Ancestry transcription "Texas, U.S., Death Certificates, 1903-1982, Certificate Number 76852 (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/2272/records/99712 : accessed 2026-11-26)": death 17 Sep 1982, age 64, birth 4 Dec 1917 in Iowa, father Ralph K Quass, mother Emma Nehls, spouse Ivyl Greenley. The death entry is primary information from the certifying official. (2) The Texas Death Index row, "Texas, Death Index, 1903-2000, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VZZJ-TBB : Wed Sep 17 17:48:07 UTC 2025), Entry for Kenneth Quass, 17 Sep 1982", which is drawn from the same certificate and is one evidence unit with it, not a second confirmation. (3) Find a Grave memorial 54602333 ("Find a Grave memorial 54602333, Kenneth Werner Quass Sr., G R Wise Gittens, Added Jul 7, 2010"), whose headstone transcription reads "KENNETH W. DEC. 4, 1917 - SEPT. 17, 1982". The headstone is a separate unit from the certificate, so the date has two independent supports. The age of 64 agrees with a 4 December 1917 birth.

## Identity
The certificate's parents (Ralph K Quass, Emma Nehls) and spouse (Ivyl Greenley) match the tree's parents and wife of Kenneth Werner Quass, as do the memorial's family list and 1917 birth date. The tree records three other men named Kenneth Quass (namesakes); parents, spouse and birth date separate this man from them. The tree also carries a September 1982 residence at Marshall, Minnesota from the Residence Database, and the certificate gives a residence of San Diego, California. Neither fixes where he was on 17 September, so neither contradicts a death in Texas that day; the move from Minnesota is unexplained by any record in the project.

## The place dispute (conflict c_001, resolved in favor of the certificate)
The certificate and the index give Grapevine, Tarrant County. The memorial's header repeats Grapevine, but its biography, written in 2010 by the decedent's son, says the certificate place is false: his father died aboard a commercial flight from Miami to San Diego, was found dead in the aircraft toilet, and reached the downtown Dallas airport; the coroner performed no autopsy and signed the son's name as informant, though the son lived in Minnesota. The son also reports a later suggestion of foul play.

Weighing: the certificate was made at the time by an official whose duty was to record place of death. The biography is secondhand (the son was in Minnesota, relying on an airline and a coroner's call), written about 28 years later, by a person who alleges forgery and has a stated motive to contest the record. No document in the project supports the flight, the lack of an autopsy or the forgery, and the memorial keeps Grapevine in its own header. Plausibility does not settle it: a death in flight followed by landing near Grapevine (DFW adjoins it) is possible, and the official may simply have recorded where the body was taken into custody. So Grapevine is preferred, but the in-flight account is not disproved. If it were true, the date would likely stand while the place of death would become an aircraft in flight, with the certificate's informant line unreliable.

## Source quality
The certificate is read only through a transcription (derivative); the uploaded certificate PDF yielded no extracted text and no certificate image was reached. The index is derivative of the same record. The memorial is derivative and secondary except for the headstone text.

## Not examined
The place rests on one certificate unit read as a transcription. Records that could raise or change the tier: the certified certificate image (Texas Bureau of Vital Statistics, or Ancestry or FamilySearch Texas, Deaths, 1977-1986 images), which would confirm the transcription and show the informant; the airline passenger or death report and the medical examiner's file for a Miami to San Diego flight about 17 September 1982, the only direct test of the in-flight account; and GenealogyBank obituaries, BillionGraves and Texas probate, which would mainly corroborate. Because the airline and medical examiner records could change the place, the place stays probable rather than proved.

## Birthplace note
Birthplace is not part of this conclusion. The tree's Sumner, Bremer, Iowa has no record basis found here; the memorial names Buchanan County, Iowa and the certificate says only Iowa.

## Tier
Probable. Date: well supported by two independent units. Place: preferred on the official certificate, with an untested, uncorroborated contrary account and a transcription-only view of the certificate. Conclusions here remain open to revision if new evidence emerges.
